To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the duration in self- employment of necessity entrepreneurs is significantly shorter than the duration of opportunity entrepreneurs.

(1) Necessity entrepreneurs have a shorter self-employment duration than opportunity entrepreneurs, but this effect is no longer significant after controlling for educational variables; (2) Opportunity entrepreneurs are more motivated by the desire to be their own boss than necessity entrepreneurs; (3) Necessity and opportunity entrepreneurs differ regarding their educational background.

the following questions: Do necessity and opportunity entrepreneurs have different durations in self-employment?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
necessity entrepreneurs do not have a significantly shorter duration of self-employment once educational variables are controlled for.
necessity entrepreneurs are more likely to fail in their self-employed business, but this result is not due to the type of motivation, but to other factors.
the effect of motivation on self-employment duration is not a robust one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
necessity entrepreneurs are more likely to leave self-employment than are opportunity entrepreneurs.
necessity entrepreneurs are not a homogeneous group and that they are not necessarily a problem group for policy makers.
the difference in duration in self-empoyment between necessity and opportunity entrepreneurs is no original effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the duration of self-employment is not a good indicator for the success of entrepreneurship policy.
the duration of necessity and opportunity entrepreneurs is similar once we control for educational variables.
the distinction between necessity and opportunity entrepreneurs has to be treated with great care.
